title: The safety scan: look before you move (part 1 of 2)
sources: docs/council-synthesis.md CD-3 (Heisman-style safety first; Kotov, Aagaard routines, recalled [R])
docs/citable-views.md 10.4-10.6 (Dan Heisman, Hope Chess and Looking for Trouble, paraphrased from secondary pages [S]; the books were not read)

positions: all boards in this lesson are authored, none taken from a game database. Those with an item replay from the start position in content/items/lesson-bg-l-loop-v1-1.json; the others are built by hand and checked by the claims on the board [V]

the Nxb5 example: [R] a trap I recall from Spanish/Berlin lines, not checked in a book here; the refutation 6...Nxb5? 7.Nxc6+ is engine-checked [V, SF19 lite d18]; the opening name is not needed for the lesson

steps.text: The pawn on e4 was the loose one. Finding it was the **safety scan**: two quick questions before every move. **One:** what did my opponent's last move attack or open up? **Two:** is any of my pieces loose? [H] My guess is the scan takes ten or fifteen seconds as a habit; I have not timed learners. A habit, not a law, built for plain dangers, not deep tactics.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's last move aimed a knight at the e-pawn. Answer one: defend it.

line.say: A pawn now defends the e-pawn, so a capture there could be answered.
Black develops a pawn of its own, and nothing of White's is loose any more.

claims.statement: Before the move, the pawn on e4 is loose.
After d3, no White piece is loose.
d3 and castling are both among the engine's top choices.

steps.caption: White to move. Answer two: take the attacker. Two bishops are attacked here, and the scan finds both.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight that was attacking the loose bishop on e4, and it also leaves the h6 pawn's reach.
Black retakes with the queen. The knight that threatened e4 is gone.

claims.statement: The bishop on e4 is loose.
One Black piece attacks the bishop on e4.
One Black piece attacks the bishop on g5 (the h6 pawn).
Bxf6 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: When a piece is attacked, three common answers are: **defend** it, so a capture can be answered; **remove the attacker**, usually by capturing it; or **move the piece away**. Two more come later: block the line, or make a bigger threat of your own. This is a teaching frame, not a complete list. You have now seen the first two. Next, the third.

steps.title: Same square, different attacker
steps.prompt: A rook attacks a defended knight. Then a pawn does. Predict, for each, whether White must react.

steps.caption: White to move. A pawn attacks the bishop on g5. Answer three: move it away.

line.say: The bishop leaves the pawn's reach and keeps its diagonal.
Black pushes a pawn to attack it again.
It steps back once more, safe from the pawns for now.

claims.statement: One Black piece attacks the bishop on g5: the pawn on h6.
On h4 nothing of Black's attacks the bishop.
Bh4 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: **Defended is not the same as safe.** Counting values are a rule of thumb: pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. If a cheaper piece attacks your defended piece, it can take, you retake, and you have lost more than you won. Ask two things: what attacks it, and what would the trade cost me?

steps.caption: Same position. Suppose White ignores the pawn on h6 and plays a quiet move on the other wing.

line.say: A quiet move that does nothing about the attack on the bishop.
The pawn takes the bishop: the knight defends g5, but a pawn is the cheapest attacker there is.
The knight retakes the pawn. White gave a bishop (3) for a pawn (1).

claims.statement: The bishop on g5 is defended once, by the knight.
Ignoring the pawn is far worse than moving the bishop.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on d5 is defended once and attacked twice. Count before you capture.

line.say: The cheaper attacker, the knight, captures first.
The pawn retakes.
The second attacker takes the pawn. White gave a knight and won a knight and a pawn.

claims.statement: Two White pieces attack the knight on d5.
One Black piece defends the knight on d5.

steps.text: Count the attackers against the defenders on the square. Here two White pieces attack the knight and one pawn defends it. The cheapest attacker captures first, so White trades a knight for a knight and then takes the pawn too. The opponent's last move is the only thing that changed since you last looked, so that is where new danger can come from. [I]

steps.caption: Black to move. The same lesson from the other side: a defended bishop attacked by a pawn.

line.say: The bishop looks active and the knight defends it.
But a pawn attacks g4, and it takes.
The knight retakes. Black gave a bishop (3) for a pawn (1).

claims.statement: After Bg4 one White piece attacks it: the pawn on h3.
Bg4 is far worse than the best move.

steps.text: The second question has a twin: **what does my own move do?** Dan Heisman, a chess coach, calls moving without checking the opponent's forcing replies (checks, captures, threats) "Hope Chess". I know this from articles about his books, not from the books themselves. After a move, look in three places: the piece that moved, the pieces it used to guard, and any line it opens.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight is attacked once and defended once. A rook move along the second rank looks harmless: who was guarding the knight?

line.say: The rook slides along the rank, and it was the only piece defending the knight on e3.
Black takes the knight, which nothing defends now. One quiet move cost a piece.

claims.statement: Before the move the rook on e2 defends the knight on e3.
After the rook leaves the e-file nothing defends the knight.
After the rook move the knight on e3 is loose.
Rd2 is far worse than the best move.

steps.caption: Black to move. The bishop on b5 is loose, and the knight can take it. Is it really free?

line.say: Black grabs the loose bishop. It looks like a free piece.
The knight on e5 was blocking the rook. Moving it uncovers check from the rook on e1, and it takes a knight on the way.
Black answers the check. With the natural block Be7, the knight on c6 now attacks the queen, and White takes it.
The knight now attacks the queen, and White takes it.

claims.statement: After the knight leaves e5, the rook on e1 attacks the king's square.
After Be7 the knight on c6 attacks the queen on d8.
Nxb5 is far worse than the best move.
Be7 and Nxe5 are both fine (within a few hundredths of a pawn at depth 16-18), while Nxb5 loses about 7 pawns [V, SF19 lite d18].

steps.text: A loose enemy piece is a chance, not an order. Run the scan on the capture itself before you take. [H] My guess, not measured: the freer a piece looks, the more it is worth one extra look, because a gift and a bait look the same from far away. Treat "free" as a question, not an answer.

**Remember.** The safety scan asks two questions before I move: what did the last move attack or open, and is any of my pieces loose? A threatened piece can be defended, saved by taking the attacker, or moved away. Defended is not the same as safe when a cheaper piece attacks it. I check my own move too, and a free-looking enemy piece gets one more look first.
